plants.name: Euphorbia pulcherrima
plants.description: Wild poinsettias grow as lanky shrubs and small trees. In winter they put out blazing crimson bracts, which are leaf-like structures that look like petals. They crown clusters of tiny, button-like yellow flowers. Short winter days trigger the color change, so the show peaks just as the holiday season begins.
plants.bloomingSeason: Winter, typically December to January, when short days of about 10-12 hours trigger color
plants.location: Southern Mexico and Central America (native range); also grown worldwide as a holiday plant
plants.funFact: The showy red parts are modified leaves, not petals. The true flowers are the tiny yellow structures in the center, called cyathia.

plants.name: Ceratopetalum gummiferum
plants.description: This bushy Australian tree is covered in sprays of small creamy flowers in early summer. After the petals drop, the sepals swell and turn a vivid rose-red. This gives bushes along the sandstone gullies and gardens of Sydney a festive glow right when the holidays arrive.
plants.bloomingSeason: Flowers appear from November to December in the Southern Hemisphere's early summer. The red sepals follow and are shed around February.
plants.funFact: The petals are tiny and fall away quickly. The red color that Australians use as Christmas decoration comes from the enlarged sepals.

plants.name: Camellia sasanqua
plants.description: A graceful, glossy-leaved evergreen shrub that brightens the cool, gray days of early winter. Its silky, often fragrant blooms open in drifts of white, blush and deep pink. They scatter petals like confetti beneath the branches, and are a welcome nectar source when little else is flowering.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late autumn into early winter, usually October or November through December or January
plants.location: Native to southern Japan; widely grown in mild temperate gardens of Asia, Europe, the Americas and Australasia
plants.funFact: Camellia sasanqua is a close relative of the tea plant, Camellia sinensis. Its seeds are pressed to make an edible oil used in Japan.
